claim: Neurons in dorsal motor cortex modulated during speaking in both participants.
source: Significant modulation was found during speaking at least one syllable (p<0.05 compared to during silence) in 73/104 T5 electrodes' TCs (13/22 SUA) and 47/101 T8 electrodes (12/25 SUA).
evidence: Statistical testing showed significant modulation with p<0.05 threshold.

claim: Active neurons were distributed throughout the area sampled by the arrays.
source: Active neurons were distributed throughout the area sampled by the arrays, and most modulated to speaking multiple syllables (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting a broadly distributed coding scheme.
evidence: Spatial distribution shown in figures and described in text.

claim: Most active neurons modulated to speaking multiple syllables.
source: Active neurons were distributed throughout the area sampled by the arrays, and most modulated to speaking multiple syllables (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting a broadly distributed coding scheme.
evidence: Quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing distribution of syllable responses.

claim: The neural activity suggests a broadly distributed coding scheme for speech.
source: Active neurons were distributed throughout the area sampled by the arrays, and most modulated to speaking multiple syllables (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting a broadly distributed coding scheme.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that neurons respond to multiple syllables.

claim: Neural modulation was significantly stronger when speaking compared to after hearing the auditory prompts.
source: modulation was significantly stronger when speaking compared to after hearing the auditory prompts: the neural population firing rate change compared to the silent condition was 4.03 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T5-syllables dataset, 2.90x for the T8-syllables dataset (Figure 1E), 6.71x higher for the T5-words dataset, and 2.12x for T8-words (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical significance testing shown in figures.

claim: The neural population firing rate change was 4.03 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T5-syllables dataset.
source: the neural population firing rate change compared to the silent condition was 4.03 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T5-syllables dataset
evidence: Specific quantitative measurement from data analysis.

claim: The neural population firing rate change was 2.90 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T8-syllables dataset.
source: 2.90x for the T8-syllables dataset (Figure 1E)
evidence: Specific quantitative measurement from data analysis.

claim: The neural population firing rate change was 6.71 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T5-words dataset.
source: 6.71x higher for the T5-words dataset
evidence: Specific quantitative measurement from data analysis.

claim: The neural population firing rate change was 2.12 times higher after the go cue compared to after the audio prompt for the T8-words dataset.
source: 2.12x for T8-words (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Specific quantitative measurement from data analysis.

claim: Neural population activity showed phonemic structure with phonemes grouped by place of articulation showing more similar neural patterns.
source: analysis of an additional dataset in which participant T5 spoke 41 different phonemes revealed that neural population activity showed phonemic structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 5): for example, when phonemes were grouped by place of articulation (Bouchard et al., 2013; Lotte et al., 2015; Moses et al., 2019), population firing rate vectors were significantly more similar between phonemes within the same group than between phonemes in different groups (p<0.001, shuffle test).
evidence: Statistical testing with shuffle control showing p<0.001.

claim: 99 of 120 electrodes that were active during speaking syllables also were active during production of at least one of seven non-speech orofacial movements.
source: In both participants, 99 of 120 electrodes that were active during speaking syllables (24 out of 25 sorted neurons) also were active during production of at least one of seven non-speech orofacial movements (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct count from experimental data.

claim: 24 out of 25 sorted neurons that were active during speaking syllables also were active during production of at least one of seven non-speech orofacial movements.
source: In both participants, 99 of 120 electrodes that were active during speaking syllables (24 out of 25 sorted neurons) also were active during production of at least one of seven non-speech orofacial movements (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct count from experimental data.

claim: Weak but significant firing rate correlations with breathing were observed.
source: We also observed weak but significant firing rate correlations with breathing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical significance demonstrated in supplementary figure.

claim: Modulation for speaking was approximately 4.7 times stronger than for unattended breathing.
source: Modulation for speaking was stronger than for unattended breathing (~4.7 x)
evidence: Quantitative comparison from data analysis.

claim: Modulation for speaking was approximately 2.6 times stronger than for instructed breathing.
source: instructed breathing (~2.6 x)
evidence: Quantitative comparison from data analysis.

claim: Modulation for attempted arm movements was approximately 2.8 times stronger than for speaking and orofacial movements.
source: modulation for attempted arm movements was stronger than for speaking and orofacial movements (~2.8 x, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative comparison from data analysis.

claim: Cross-validated prediction accuracies for syllables were 84.6% for T5 with mean chance accuracy of 10.1%.
source: Cross-validated prediction accuracies for syllables were 84.6% for T5 (10 classes, mean chance accuracy was 10.1% across shuffle controls)
evidence: Decoding performance measured with cross-validation and shuffle controls.

claim: Cross-validated prediction accuracies for syllables were 54.7% for T8 with mean chance accuracy of 8.6%.
source: 54.7% for T8 (11 classes, chance was 8.6%)
evidence: Decoding performance measured with cross-validation and shuffle controls.

claim: Word decoding accuracies were 83.5% for T5 with mean chance accuracy of 9.1%.
source: Word decoding accuracies were 83.5% for T5 (11 classes, chance was 9.1%)
evidence: Decoding performance measured with cross-validation and shuffle controls.

claim: Word decoding accuracies were 61.5% for T8 with mean chance accuracy of 9.3%.
source: 61.5% for T8 (11 classes, chance was 9.3%)
evidence: Decoding performance measured with cross-validation and shuffle controls.

claim: Classification accuracies for neural activity 0 to 500 ms after the speech prompt were only marginally better than chance.
source: We also used the same method to decode neural activity from 0 to 500 ms after the speech prompt and found that classification accuracies were only marginally better than chance (overall accuracies between 11.1% and 16.6% across the four datasets, p<0.05 versus shuffle controls in three of the four datasets; Figure 3C gray bars).
evidence: Statistical comparison to shuffle controls.

claim: The largest dPCA component summarizing neural activity during movement initiation was 98.7% condition-invariant in participant T5.
source: Like in Kaufman et al. (2016), the largest dPCA component summarizing each participants' neural activity during movement initiation was largely CI: this component was 98.7% CI in participant T5
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dPCA analysis.

claim: The largest dPCA component summarizing neural activity during movement initiation was 87.3% condition-invariant in participant T8.
source: 87.3% CI in participant T8 (Figure 4A)
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dPCA analysis.

claim: The CIS1 component rapidly increased after the go cue and was essentially identical regardless of which word was spoken in T5.
source: Figure 4B shows that in T5, this 'CIS1' component, which rapidly increased after the go cue, was essentially identical regardless of which word was spoken.
evidence: Visual and quantitative demonstration in Figure 4B.

claim: In T8, the CIS1 was not as cleanly condition-invariant as in T5, but nonetheless showed a similar increase following the go cue for each word.
source: In T8, the CIS1 was not as cleanly condition-invariant, but nonetheless showed a similar increase following the go cue for each word.
evidence: Observation from data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Condition-invariant neural population activity component was found in all six datasets examined (T5 and T8 syllables, T5 and T8 words, and two T5 replication datasets).
source: We also found this condition-invariant neural population activity component in all four additional datasets that we examined: T5's and T8's syllables task datasets, as well as two additional replication datasets in which participant T5 spoke just five of the words (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Consistent finding across multiple independent datasets.

claim: Rotatory dynamics could explain substantial variance in how population activity evolved moment-by-moment during speaking in participant T5.
source: In participant T5, all conditions' neural state trajectories rotated in the same direction (similarly to Churchland et al., 2012; Pandarinath et al., 2015), and rotatory dynamics could explain substantial variance in how population activity evolved moment-by-moment during speaking.
evidence: jPCA analysis showing rotatory structure in neural trajectories.

claim: Rotatory structure was significantly stronger than expected by chance in T5's speaking data.
source: Application of a recent population dynamics hypothesis testing method (Elsayed and Cunningham, 2017) revealed that this rotatory structure was significantly stronger than expected by chance in T5's speaking data
evidence: Statistical testing using tensor maximum entropy method.

claim: Rotatory structure was not significantly stronger than expected by chance in T8's speaking data.
source: Application of a recent population dynamics hypothesis testing method (Elsayed and Cunningham, 2017) revealed that this rotatory structure was significantly stronger than expected by chance in T5's speaking data, but not in T8's speaking data (Figure 5B)
evidence: Statistical testing using tensor maximum entropy method.

claim: Rotatory dynamics were not observed when the same jPCA analysis was applied to neural activity following the audio prompt.
source: or when this analysis was applied to neural activity following the audio prompt (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: Control analysis showing specificity of rotatory dynamics to speech production epoch.

claim: Speech-related activity has not previously been reported in the dorsal 'hand knob' motor cortex area.
source: Speech-related activity has not previously been reported in this cortical area
evidence: Literature review indicating novelty of finding.

claim: A meta-analysis of imaging studies indicates that responses are occasionally seen in dorsal motor cortex during speaking tasks.
source: Although imaging experiments consistently identify ventral cortical activation during speaking tasks, a meta-analysis of such studies (Guenther, 2016) indicates that responses are occasionally seen (though not, to our knowledge, explicitly called out) in dorsal motor cortex.
evidence: Citation to meta-analysis by Guenther, 2016.

claim: Behavioral, transcranial magnetic stimulation, and electrical stimulation mapping studies have reported interactions between motor control of the hand and mouth.
source: Additionally, behavioral (Gentilucci and Campione, 2011; Vainio et al., 2013), transcranial magnetic stimulation studies (Devlin and Watkins, 2007; Meister et al., 2003), and electrical stimulation mapping studies (Breshears et al., 2018) have reported interactions (and interference) between motor control of the hand and mouth.
evidence: Multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The close linkage between hand and speech networks has been hypothesized to be due to a need for hand-mouth coordination and an evolutionary relationship between manual and articulatory gestures.
source: This close linkage between hand and speech networks has been hypothesized to be due to a need for hand-mouth coordination and an evolutionary relationship between manual and articulatory gestures (Gentilucci and Stefani, 2012; Rizzolatti and Arbib, 1998).
evidence: Citations to theoretical papers proposing this hypothesis.

claim: The presence of neurons responding to mouth and tongue movements in the dorsal 'arm and hand' area of motor cortex indicates that sensorimotor maps for different body parts are more widespread and overlapping than previously thought.
source: The presence of neurons responding to mouth and tongue movements in the dorsal 'arm and hand' area of motor cortex indicates that sensorimotor maps for different body parts are even more widespread and overlapping than previously thought.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental findings in context of prior knowledge.

claim: The conventional model of a 'motor homunculus' division by major body regions may not extend to the single-neuron scale.
source: Neurons modulated during speaking and during non-speaking movements of the tongue, lips, and jaw. This challenges whether the conventional model of a 'motor homunculus' division by major body regions extends to the single-neuron scale.
evidence: Inference from finding that individual neurons respond to both speech and non-speech movements.

claim: Spoken words and syllables could be decoded from single trials.
source: Spoken words and syllables could be decoded from single trials, demonstrating the potential of intracortical recordings for brain-computer interfaces to restore speech.
evidence: Demonstrated by decoding analysis with high accuracy.

claim: Intracortical recordings show potential for brain-computer interfaces to restore speech.
source: Spoken words and syllables could be decoded from single trials, demonstrating the potential of intracortical recordings for brain-computer interfaces to restore speech.
evidence: Inference from successful decoding results.

claim: A component that was mostly invariant across initiating different words was present during speaking.
source: Two neural population dynamics features previously reported for arm movements were also present during speaking: a component that was mostly invariant across initiating different words, followed by rotatory dynamics during speaking.
evidence: Demonstrated through dPCA analysis.

claim: Rotatory dynamics during speaking were present following the condition-invariant component.
source: Two neural population dynamics features previously reported for arm movements were also present during speaking: a component that was mostly invariant across initiating different words, followed by rotatory dynamics during speaking.
evidence: Demonstrated through jPCA analysis.

claim: Common neural dynamical motifs may underlie movement of arm and speech articulators.
source: This suggests that common neural dynamical motifs may underlie movement of arm and speech articulators.
evidence: Inference from finding similar dynamics in speech and arm movements.

claim: Participant T5 was diagnosed with C4 AIS-C spinal cord injury 10 years prior to the study.
source: Participant 'T5' (male, right-handed, 64 years old at the time of the study) was diagnosed with C4 AIS-C spinal cord injury 10 years prior to these research sessions.
evidence: Participant demographic information.

claim: Participant T8 was diagnosed with C4 AIS-A spinal cord injury 11 years prior to the study.
source: Participant 'T8' (male, right-handed, 56 years old at the time of the study) was diagnosed with ﻿C4 AIS-A spinal cord injury 11 years prior to these sessions.
evidence: Participant demographic information.

claim: T5 retained the ability to weakly flex his left elbow and fingers and some slight and inconsistent residual movement of both the upper and lower extremities.
source: ﻿He retained the ability to weakly flex his left elbow and fingers and some slight and inconsistent residual movement of both the upper and lower extremities.
evidence: Clinical assessment of participant abilities.

claim: T5 was able to speak normally and converse naturally without hearing assistance.
source: T5 was able to speak normally and converse naturally without hearing assistance, but had some trouble hearing from his left ear.
evidence: Clinical assessment of participant abilities.

claim: T8 retained restricted and non-functional voluntary shoulder girdle motion on both sides, and non-functional voluntary finger extension on his left side.
source: He retained restricted and non-functional voluntary shoulder girdle motion on both sides, and non-functional voluntary finger extension on his left side.
evidence: Clinical assessment of participant abilities.

claim: T8 was able to speak normally and converse naturally with the assistance of hearing aids in both his ears.
source: T8 was able to speak normally and converse naturally with the assistance of hearing aids in both his ears.
evidence: Clinical assessment of participant abilities.

claim: The electrode arrays were placed in dorsal 'hand knob' area of motor cortex.
source: the electrode arrays were in dorsal 'hand knob' area of motor cortex
evidence: Surgical placement information.

claim: The electrode arrays strongly modulated to participants' attempted movement of their arm and hand.
source: which we previously found to strongly modulate to these participants' attempted movement of their arm and hand (Ajiboye et al., 2017; Brandman et al., 2018; Pandarinath et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to prior studies from the same research group.

claim: T5 and T8 had arrays placed 14 and 34 months, respectively, prior to the syllables and words tasks.
source: T5 and T8 had arrays placed 14 and 34 months, respectively, prior to the present study's prompted words, syllables, and orofacial movements tasks.
evidence: Timeline information for the study.

claim: The T5-breathing and T5-comparisons datasets were recorded 26 months after array placement.
source: The T5-breathing and T5-comparisons datasets were recorded 26 months after array placement
evidence: Timeline information for the study.

claim: The T5-5words-A and T5-5words-B datasets were recorded 28 months after array placement.
source: the T5-5words-A and T5-5words-B datasets were recorded 28 months after array placement
evidence: Timeline information for the study.

claim: The T5-phonemes dataset was recorded 29 months after array placement.
source: the T5-phonemes dataset was recorded 29 months after array placement
evidence: Timeline information for the study.

claim: Decoding mistakes and low-dimensional representations tended to follow phonetic similarities.
source: Decoding mistakes (Figure 3B) and low-dimensional representations (Figure 3A) tended to follow phonetic similarities (e.g. ba and ga, a and ae).
evidence: Observation from decoding analysis and visualization.

claim: The observation of neural correlate similarities is consistent with previous ECoG studies.
source: This observation is consistent with previous ECoG studies (Bouchard et al., 2013; Cheung et al., 2016; Livezey et al., 2019; Moses et al., 2019; Mugler et al., 2014)
evidence: Comparison to prior literature.

claim: Larger neural differences were observed between unvoiced k and p and the beginning of their voiced counterparts at the start of ga and ba, suggesting strong laryngeal tuning.
source: although the larger neural differences we observed between unvoiced k and p and the beginning of their voiced counterparts at the start of ga and ba suggests strong laryngeal tuning (Dichter et al., 2018).
evidence: Observation from data with citation to related work.

claim: Neural correlate similarities may reflect similarities in the underlying articulator movements.
source: These neural correlate similarities may reflect similarities in the underlying articulator movements (Chartier et al., 2018; Lotte et al., 2015; Mugler et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Neural state rotations occurred after the condition invariant translation.
source: Neural state rotations occurred after the condition invariant translation
evidence: Temporal relationship observed in Videos 2 and 3.

claim: In monkey arm reaching data, neural rotations either partially overlapped with, or more immediately followed, the CIS shift.
source: by comparison, in Kaufman et al. (2016) the neural rotations also lagged the CIS shift, but in the monkey arm reaching data these rotations either partially overlapped with, or more immediately followed, the CIS shift.
evidence: Comparison to prior study by Kaufman et al. (2016).

claim: The CIS1 and jPCA dimensions were largely orthogonal in these data.
source: We note that existing models of how a condition-invariant signal 'kicks' dynamics into a different state space region where rotatory dynamics unfold (Kaufman et al., 2016; Sussillo et al., 2015) do not require that the CIS and rotatory dynamics must be orthogonal, but in these data we did observed that the CIS1 and jPCA dimensions were largely orthogonal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Dorsal motor cortex may participate in neural computations underlying speech production.
source: First, these data suggest that 'hand knob' motor cortex, an area not previously known to be active during speaking (Breshears et al., 2015; Dichter et al., 2018; Leuthardt et al., 2011; Lotte et al., 2015), may in fact participate, or at least receive correlates of, neural computations underlying speech production.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings with citations to prior work.

claim: Speech-related single-neuron modulation might have been missed by previous studies due to the coarser resolution of ECoG.
source: Speech-related single-neuron modulation might have been missed by previous studies due to the coarser resolution of ECoG (Chan et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculation about why prior studies did not observe this, with citation.

claim: The familiar 'motor homunculus' is overly simplistic.
source: If this finding holds true in the wider population, this would underscore that the familiar 'motor homunculus' (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937) is overly simplistic.
evidence: Inference from findings with citation to original homunculus work.

claim: Motor cortex does not rigidly follow a sequential point-to-point somatotopy.
source: It is generally recognized that motor cortex does not rigidly follow a sequential point-to-point somatotopy
evidence: Statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Penfield and colleagues were aware that the motor homunculus was a simplified summary and intended it as such.
source: and indeed, Penfield and colleagues were aware of this and intended for their diagram to be a simplified summary of results showing partially overlapping motor fields that also varied substantially across individuals (Catani, 2017).
evidence: Historical context with citation.

claim: The current view of precentral gyrus organization features a dorsal-to-ventral progression and separation of the major body regions (leg, arm, head).
source: However, the patchy mosaicism amongst nearby body parts in the current view of precentral gyrus organization still features a dorsal-to-ventral progression and separation of the major body regions (leg, arm, head) (Farrell et al., 2007; Schieber, 2001).
evidence: Statement of current scientific understanding with citations.

claim: Activity from these same arrays encodes intended arm and hand movements.
source: Given our previous finding that activity from these same arrays encodes intended arm and hand movements (Pandarinath et al., 2017)
evidence: Citation to prior work from the same research group.

claim: The observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the systems for speech and manual gestures are interlocked.
source: these observations are consistent with the hypothesis that the systems for speech and manual gestures are interlocked (Gentilucci and Stefani, 2012; Rizzolatti and Arbib, 1998; Vainio et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference with citations to theoretical papers.

claim: Neurons in this area also modulate during attempted movements of the neck and legs.
source: However, emerging work from our group showing that neurons in this area also modulate during attempted movements of the ﻿neck and legs (Willett et al., 2019)
evidence: Citation to ongoing work from the same research group.

claim: Much of the body may be represented (to varying strengths) in dorsal motor cortex.
source: suggests that much of the body is represented (to varying strengths) in dorsal motor cortex.
evidence: Inference from multiple observations.

claim: The observed neural overlap between hand and speech articulators may be a consequence of distributed whole-body coding, rather than a privileged speech-manual linkage.
source: Thus, the observed neural overlap between hand and speech articulators may be a consequence of distributed whole-body coding, rather than a privileged speech-manual linkage.
evidence: Alternative interpretation of findings.

claim: The observed neural activity reflects movements of the speech articulators (the tongue, lips, jaw, and larynx).
source: Our data suggest that the observed neural activity reflects movements of the speech articulators (the tongue, lips, jaw, and larynx)
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence presented in the study.

claim: Cortical remapping due to tetraplegia is unlikely to explain the results.
source: While we cannot rule this out, we believe that remapping of face representation to the hand knob area is unlikely.
evidence: Authors' interpretation with supporting arguments.

claim: The sites recorded from still strongly modulate during attempted hand and arm movements despite many years of paralysis.
source: Despite these participants' many years of paralysis, the sites we recorded from still strongly modulate during attempted hand and arm movements (Ajiboye et al., 2017; Brandman et al., 2018; Pandarinath et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to prior studies showing continued arm/hand representation.

claim: Modulation during attempted arm movements was stronger than during speech production in participant T5.
source: We also verified in participant T5 that modulation during attempted arm movements was stronger than during speech production.
evidence: Direct comparison performed in the study.

claim: Motor cortical remapping following arm amputation was recently shown to be smaller than previously thought.
source: Furthermore, motor cortical remapping following arm amputation was recently shown to be smaller than previously thought (Wesselink et al., 2019)
evidence: Citation to recent study on remapping.

claim: Motor cortical remapping following arm amputation is much smaller than what would be needed to move lip representations to hand cortex.
source: and in particular much smaller than what would be needed to move lip representations to hand cortex (Makin et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation with specific interpretation.

claim: Cortical reorganization following injury in adults is more limited than previously thought.
source: On the sensory side, emerging evidence suggests that cortical reorganization following injury in adults is more limited than previously thought (Makin and Bensmaia, 2017)
evidence: Citation to review article.

claim: A recent microstimulation study in the hand somatosensory cortex of a person with tetraplegia did not find functional reorganization.
source: and a recent microstimulation study in the hand somatosensory cortex of a person with tetraplegia did not find functional reorganization (Flesher et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to specific study.

claim: Definitively resolving the ambiguity about remapping would require intracortical recording from this eloquent brain area in able-bodied people.
source: While these threads of evidence argue against remapping, definitively resolving this ambiguity would require intracortical recording from this eloquent brain area in able-bodied people.
evidence: Authors' statement about limitations and future work needed.

claim: Speech is spared following lesions in the dorsal motor cortex area.
source: Speech is spared following lesions in this area (Chen et al., 2006; Tei, 1999), indicating that it is not necessary for speech production.
evidence: Citations to clinical studies.

claim: Dorsal motor cortex is not necessary for speech production.
source: Speech is spared following lesions in this area (Chen et al., 2006; Tei, 1999), indicating that it is not necessary for speech production.
evidence: Inference from lesion studies.

claim: Dorsal motor cortex may play some supporting role in speaking, perhaps contributing to more demanding speaking tasks.
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that dorsal motor cortex plays some supporting role in speaking, perhaps contributing to more demanding speaking tasks
evidence: Speculation about possible function.

claim: The activity may reflect speech efference copy for coordinating orofacial and upper extremity movements.
source: or that this activity reflects speech efference copy for coordinating orofacial and upper extremity movements.
evidence: Alternative speculation about function.

claim: High dimensional representations resulting from mixed selectivity enable more complex computations.
source: This would be in line with theoretical arguments that high dimensional representations resulting from mixed selectivity – in this case, both within major body regions (a given neuron being tuned for multiple arm movements or for multiple orofacial movements) and across major body regions (neurons being tuned for both arm and face movements) – enable more complex computations (Fusi et al., 2016)
evidence: Citation to theoretical paper.

claim: Intracortical recordings show promise as signal sources for BCIs to restore speech to people with some forms of anarthria.
source: Our second main finding is that, based on offline decoding results, intracortical recordings show promise as signal sources for BCIs to restore speech to people with some forms of anarthria.
evidence: Inference from decoding results.

claim: Decoding the neural correlates of attempted speech production may be more desirable than approaches that decode covert internal speech or more abstract elements of language.
source: Decoding the neural correlates of attempted speech production (Brumberg et al., 2011) into audible sounds or text may be more desirable than approaches that decode covert internal speech (Leuthardt et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2016) or more abstract elements of language (Chan et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2017) because decoding attempted movements leverages existing neural machinery that separates internal monologue and speech preparation from intentional speaking.
evidence: Argument with citations to alternative approaches.

claim: The present results compare favorably to previously published decoding accuracies using ECoG.
source: The present results compare favorably to previously published decoding accuracies using ECoG (Mugler et al., 2014; Ramsey et al., 2018)
evidence: Comparison to prior literature.

claim: The dorsal recording locations are likely suboptimal for decoding speech.
source: despite our dorsal recording locations likely being suboptimal for decoding speech.
evidence: Authors' interpretation based on known speech areas.

claim: Multi-electrode arrays placed in ventral motor cortex would be expected to yield even better decoding accuracies.
source: Multi-electrode arrays placed in ventral motor cortex would be expected to yield even better decoding accuracies.
evidence: Speculation based on known speech motor areas.

claim: Recent advances in the number of recording sites on intracortical probes point to a path for scaling the number of distinct sources of information for speech BCIs.
source: Furthermore, recent order-of-magnitude advances in the number of recording sites on intracortical probes (Jun et al., 2017) point to a path that stretches far forward in terms of scaling the number of distinct sources of information (neurons) for speech BCIs.
evidence: Citation to technological advance with inference about implications.

claim: The results are only a first step in establishing the feasibility of speech BCIs using intracortical electrode arrays.
source: That said, these results are only a first step in establishing the feasibility of speech BCIs using intracortical electrode arrays.
evidence: Authors' statement about limitations.

claim: Future studies will be needed to assess how well intracortical signals can be used to discriminate between a wider set of phonemes.
source: We decoded amongst a limited set of discrete syllables and words in participants who are able to speak; future studies will be needed to assess how well intracortical signals can be used to discriminate between a wider set of phonemes (Brumberg et al., 2011; Mugler et al., 2014)
evidence: Authors' statement about future work needed.

claim: Future studies will be needed to assess decoding in the absence of overt speech.
source: in the absence of overt speech (Brumberg et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2016)
evidence: Authors' statement about future work needed with citations.

claim: Future studies will be needed to assess synthesis of continuous speech.
source: and to synthesize continuous speech (Akbari et al., 2019; Anumanchipalli et al., 2019; Makin et al., 2019).
evidence: Authors' statement about future work needed with citations.

claim: Worse decoding performance was observed in participant T8.
source: We also observed worse decoding performance in participant T8
evidence: Direct observation from results.

claim: There is a need for future studies in additional participants to sample the distribution of how much speech-related neural modulation can be expected.
source: highlighting the need for future studies in additional participants to sample the distribution of how much speech-related neural modulation can be expected, and what speech BCI performance these signals can support.
evidence: Authors' statement about limitations and future work needed.

claim: Two motor cortical population dynamical motifs present during arm movements were significant features of speech activity.
source: Our third main finding is that two motor cortical population dynamical motifs present during arm movements were also significant features of speech activity.
evidence: Summary of findings from population dynamics analyses.

claim: A large condition-invariant change at movement initiation was observed in both participants.
source: We observed a large condition-invariant change at movement initiation in both participants
evidence: Result from dPCA analysis.

claim: Rotatory dynamics during movement generation were observed in one of two participants whose arrays recorded substantially more modulation.
source: and rotatory dynamics during movement generation in the one of two participants whose arrays recorded substantially more modulation.
evidence: Result from jPCA analysis.

claim: Neural state rotations may be well-suited for generating descending muscle commands driving the out-and-back articulator movements that form the kinematic building blocks of speech.
source: We speculate that these neural state rotations are well-suited for generating descending muscle commands driving the out-and-back articulator movements that form the kinematic building blocks of speech (Chartier et al., 2018; Mugler et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculation with citations to supporting work.

claim: The presence of these dynamics during both reaching and speaking could indicate a conserved computational mechanism that is ubiquitously deployed across multiple behaviors.
source: The presence of these dynamics during both reaching and speaking could indicate a conserved computational mechanism that is ubiquitously deployed across multiple behaviors to shift the circuit dynamics from withholding movement to generating the appropriate muscle commands from an oscillatory basis set.
evidence: Speculation about computational principles.

claim: There is emerging evidence that rotatory dynamics may be absent in movements with a greater role of sensory feedback, such as hand grasping.
source: For instance, there is emerging evidence that rotatory dynamics may be absent in movements with a greater role of sensory feedback, such as hand grasping (Suresh et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to recent work suggesting boundary conditions.

claim: It is unresolved whether these dynamics in dorsal motor cortex play a causal role in speaking and/or echo similar dynamics in other areas.
source: This interpretation should also be tempered by the major unresolved question of whether these dynamics in dorsal motor cortex play a causal role in speaking and/or echo similar dynamics in other areas, such as ventral motor cortex, which are more directly involved in speech (Bouchard et al., 2013).
